lessons.title: Introduction to Microsoft Word
objectives: Explain the purpose and location of Starting and closing Word and Blank Document.
Independently produce My First Microsoft Word Document using the stated requirements.
Inspect the saved output and correct common errors.
lessons.introduction: A saved, named document can be reopened and revised without retyping school work. Word is a word processor for letters, reports, resumes and projects; it is not the same as the Windows file manager.
lessons.explanation:
Ribbon: The tabbed command area above the document. A tab contains related command groups.

Document: The editable file containing text, formatting and other objects.

Save: Writes changes to the current file; Save As creates a separately named copy or changes file type.

Zoom: Changes on-screen magnification without changing printed text size.
lessons.guided_practice:
Follow the numbered demonstration on a disposable copy. After each command, explain what changed and compare with the before state.

1. Start the authorized Microsoft Word desktop application from Start; choose Blank Document.
2. Locate the title bar, Home tab, Font and Paragraph groups, document area and status bar. Use View > Ruler if the ruler is hidden.
3. Type the exercise title, press Enter once, then type the paragraph below. Use the scroll bar and zoom slider to inspect the page.
4. Choose File > Save As > Browse (or your school-approved location). Enter My_First_Word_Document and select Word Document (.docx).
5. Press Ctrl+S after editing. Close Word using File > Close or the window Close button.
6. Reopen Word > File > Open > Browse. Choose the saved file, read the title and paragraph, and confirm the saved filename.

objectives: Explain the purpose and location of Selecting and highlighting text and Cut, Copy and Paste.

lessons.introduction: Formatting a selected range creates a clear reading hierarchy. Character formatting changes letters; paragraph alignment changes the paragraph. Selecting the correct range prevents accidental changes to the whole document.
lessons.explanation:
Selection: The highlighted range that receives the next command.

Bold: Makes the selected characters thicker; Home > Font > Bold or Ctrl+B.

Highlight: Adds a marker-like background behind text; it differs from font color.

Format Painter: Copies formatting from one selection to another without copying the words.
lessons.guided_practice:
Follow the numbered demonstration on a disposable copy. After each command, explain what changed and compare with the before state.

1. Drag across SCHOOL ANNOUNCEMENT. In Home > Font choose a readable font, set 18 pt and click Bold. Center the title with Home > Paragraph > Center.
2. Select only the title and open Font Color; choose a dark, readable color. Compare the selection with unselected text.
3. Select Friday at 8:00 AM and press Ctrl+B. Select the participation sentence and press Ctrl+I.
4. Select cleaning materials and apply Text Highlight Color. Practice Underline with Ctrl+U on a temporary practice phrase, then undo it if not needed.
5. Select the body paragraph; Ctrl+C copies without removal. Move below it, press Ctrl+V, then Ctrl+Z to remove the duplicate. Ctrl+Y repeats the undone edit; undo once more to keep a single paragraph.
6. On a scratch line try font/size, Change Case, x² using Superscript and H₂O using Subscript. Try Format Painter and Clear All Formatting. Delete the scratch line before submitting.
7. Use Backspace to remove the character before the cursor and Delete for the character after it. Use Ctrl+X only when you intend to move text. Press Ctrl+S.

lessons.title: Paragraph Formatting
objectives: Explain the purpose and location of Paragraphs and paragraph marks and Left, Center, Right and Justify.
Independently produce My Daily School Routine using the stated requirements.
Inspect the saved output and correct common errors.
lessons.introduction: Paragraph settings control alignment, line spacing and indentation consistently. Using paragraph commands instead of repeated spaces and blank lines makes a document easier to revise and read.
lessons.explanation:
Paragraph: A block ending at an Enter paragraph mark. Soft-wrapped lines remain one paragraph.

Line spacing: Vertical distance between lines inside a paragraph.

Paragraph spacing: Space before or after an entire paragraph; different from line spacing.

Hanging indent: The first line stays farther left while subsequent lines move inward.
lessons.guided_practice:
Follow the numbered demonstration on a disposable copy. After each command, explain what changed and compare with the before state.

1. Type the title and one paragraph about your school day. Turn Home > Show/Hide ¶ on to see paragraph endings.
2. Click in the title paragraph and choose Center. Click in the body paragraph and choose Justify. Compare Left, Center and Right on a practice copy.
3. Select the body paragraph. Home > Paragraph > Line and Paragraph Spacing > 1.5 changes line spacing.
4. Open the Paragraph dialog. Set a first-line indent of 1.27 cm (0.5 inch); choose a small consistent After spacing, such as 6 pt. Do not indent with five spaces.
5. Type each routine item on its own paragraph. Select the five items and choose Numbering. Type the supplies on separate paragraphs and choose Bullets.
6. On a scratch bibliography paragraph set Special > Hanging and compare its first and remaining lines. Try left/right indents and a two-level list using Multilevel List.
7. Select a paragraph, apply light Shading and a visible Bottom Border. Keep text readable and restore any scratch examples not required by your final document.

2. Justify the paragraph; apply 1.5 line spacing, first-line indent and deliberate paragraph spacing.
3. Create the five-item automatic numbered routine and five-item bulleted supply list.
4. Use a readable border or shading to distinguish one paragraph; save.

lessons.introduction: Page layout determines the physical page, while headers and footers repeat useful information. Previewing the actual pages catches clipped text and accidental blank pages before printing.
lessons.explanation:
Margin: The empty area between page edges and main text.

Orientation: Portrait is taller than wide; Landscape is wider than tall.

Page break: Starts a new page without repeatedly pressing Enter.

Header footer: Areas above and below main text that can repeat across pages.

4. Insert > Header: type the school name. Insert > Page Number: choose a footer location and confirm numbers appear automatically.
5. Design > Page Borders adds a simple page border. If testing Page Color, keep readable contrast and understand printer background settings may differ.
6. Use Insert > Page Break to deliberately start a new page where appropriate. File > Print opens Print Preview; inspect all pages, margins and page numbers without sending a print job.

lessons.title: Pictures, Shapes, Text Boxes, and Tables
objectives: Explain the purpose and location of Insert picture and Resize and Crop.

lessons.introduction: Objects and tables organize a document visually. Keeping images proportional and choosing deliberate wrapping prevents pictures from covering text or distorting when the page changes.
lessons.explanation:
Text wrapping: Controls how text flows around an object; In Line with Text treats it like a character.

Crop: Hides unwanted outer parts without stretching the image.

Merge cells: Combines selected neighboring cells into a single cell.

Alt text: A useful description of a meaningful image for readers who cannot see it.
lessons.guided_practice:
Follow the numbered demonstration on a disposable copy. After each command, explain what changed and compare with the before state.

1. Insert > Table: choose two columns and five rows. Put Name, Grade/Year, Section, Adviser and Contact Number in the left column and fictional data in the right.
2. Use Table Design > Table Styles and a clear header. In Table Layout practice Insert Below, Delete Rows, Merge Cells and Split Cells on a temporary copy.
3. Insert > Pictures: choose an image you are allowed to use. Drag a corner handle to resize proportionally; Picture Format > Crop trims unnecessary edges.
4. Choose Layout Options > Square for a movable picture; compare In Line with Text. Position it so no text is hidden. Add alt text to a meaningful image.
5. Insert > Text Box: add Welcome to Microsoft Word! Insert one simple shape, then choose Shape Fill and Shape Outline.
6. Try WordArt and Icons if your Word edition offers them; retain only useful decoration. Check the table and picture in Print Preview and save.

lessons.introduction: Consistent table headings, numeric alignment and controlled widths let readers compare school records accurately. Section breaks and tab stops solve layout problems that repeated spaces cannot.
lessons.explanation:

Cell alignment: Positions cell content vertically and horizontally.

Tab stop: A defined position reached by Tab instead of many spaces.

Section break: Separates page-formatting regions; it is not the same as a page break.

lessons.introduction: References credit sources and let readers locate evidence. Automatic contents, captions and cross-references update more reliably than typed page numbers.
lessons.explanation:
Citation: A short source reference attached to the claim it supports.

Bibliography: A generated list of the sources recorded for the document.

Footnote: A note linked to a marker, normally at the bottom of the page.

Caption: A numbered label associated with a figure or table.
lessons.guided_practice:

3. Place the cursor after the relevant claim and Insert Citation. Never invent an author or source just to satisfy a count.
4. References > Insert Footnote adds an explanatory note; compare Endnote for notes at the end of a section/document.
5. Insert an authorized image, then References > Insert Caption; use a meaningful Figure caption.
6. At the beginning choose References > Table of Contents > Automatic Table. Insert a Bibliography at the end.
7. Insert a cross-reference to the figure, change a heading and update the contents/fields. Confirm no broken reference is printed.

objectives: Explain the purpose and location of Comments and Track Changes.
Independently produce Reviewed One-page Report using the stated requirements.

lessons.introduction: Track Changes records proposed edits separately from comments. Review decisions, document inspection and accessibility checks prepare a responsible final copy without silently exposing revision history.
lessons.explanation:
Tracked change: A recorded insertion, deletion or formatting proposal.

Comment: A discussion note that does not itself replace the document text.

Compare: Shows differences between two versions.

Mark as Final: A status discouraging accidental edits, not a security boundary.
lessons.guided_practice:
Follow the numbered demonstration on a disposable copy. After each command, explain what changed and compare with the before state.

1. Write a one-page school report and save an original copy. Review > Track Changes turns revision tracking on.
2. Make at least five identifiable edits. Add three useful comments tied to relevant text.
3. Review changes one by one: Accept two, Reject one, and retain other tracked edits in the review copy. Explain each decision in the reflection.
4. Review > Compare compares the original and revised versions. Discuss Combine for collecting reviewer revisions and co-authoring only in an authorized shared environment.
5. Run Review > Check Accessibility (or the available Accessibility command) and correct missing alt text, poor headings and simple table problems.
6. On a separate final copy, File > Info > Check for Issues > Inspect Document identifies personal metadata and hidden content. Review before removing information; do not destroy the evidence copy.
7. Discuss Restrict Editing, Mark as Final and digital signatures: each solves a different problem. Do not claim these replace access controls or encryption.

objectives: Explain the purpose and location of Fields and Quick Parts.
Independently produce Automated Report Formatting using the stated requirements.
Inspect the saved output and correct common errors.
lessons.introduction: Fields and reusable content reduce repeated work. A small self-recorded formatting macro can demonstrate automation, but macro-enabled files must be handled cautiously and never used to bypass Office security.
lessons.explanation:
Field: A value Word can generate or update, such as a date or document property.

Quick Parts: Reusable content or fields inserted from the Insert tab.

Macro: A recorded or written series of commands; macro-enabled documents use .docm.

VBA: The programming environment behind many Office macros; this lesson limits work to simple local formatting.
lessons.guided_practice:
Follow the numbered demonstration on a disposable copy. After each command, explain what changed and compare with the before state.

1. Create headings and body paragraphs. Insert > Quick Parts > Document Property adds a title/author property where available. Insert Date & Time and compare a fixed date with an updating date field.
2. Save a reusable heading or signature block with Quick Parts/AutoText where available. Insert it into another practice location and compare with normal copy/paste.
3. Save an initial .docx. In your school-authorized Word desktop environment, View > Macros > Record Macro names FormatPracticeHeading and stores it in this practice document, not Normal.dotm.
4. While recording, apply one safe heading format to selected text using the ribbon, then Stop Recording. Do not record file, network, shell or personal-data operations.
5. If school policy allows, select a different practice heading and run only the macro you just recorded. Verify that it formats the selection consistently. If macros are blocked, keep protections enabled and submit the recording plan and nonmacro formatting evidence instead.
6. Save as Word Macro-Enabled Document (.docm) only when a local recording exists. Inspect its VBA code with teacher supervision to relate recorded commands to formatting actions. Do not enable unknown macros or change Trust Center security.
